audio.title: Audio
audio.extraNote: For speakers whose delay the browser does not know about, for example over Bluetooth (often 150 to 300 ms). The app starts sending earlier by this amount so the sound arrives on time. Use the latency measurement in the Lab to find the right value: add the measured deviation to the current value and measure again, it should then be close to 0. 0 turns the extra latency off.

lab.qsoActive: A QSO is running. Press Stop first, then measure.
lab.level.title: Level test
lab.level.text: The device plays a test tone for three seconds and records it with its own microphone, after measuring two seconds of silence. With two devices, set the volume here first: device A plays, device B stands beside it and does not measure itself but watches the waterfall in the QSO tab.
lab.level.tone: Playing test tone and measuring (4 s) …
lab.level.verdict.gut: Level is fine: well above the noise, no overload.
lab.level.verdict.laut: Level a bit high (peak above −6 dBFS). Lower the volume slightly.
lab.level.verdict.uebersteuert: Overloaded. Lower the volume or the distance, otherwise the signal gets distorted.
lab.level.verdict.zu_leise: Too quiet or too much noise (distance below 30 dB). Raise the volume or move closer.
lab.level.verdict.kein_ton: No test tone heard. Speaker on? Microphone close enough? With headphones nothing arrives.
lab.lat.title: Delay measurement
lab.lat.text: The device sends a chirp (0.3 s, 600 to 2400 Hz) five times from its own speaker to its own microphone and measures how far the recording time deviates from the planned send time. This is the offset that later shows up as DT in a QSO. Output and input are measured together, not separately.
lab.lat.none: The chirp was never found. Do the level test first: too quiet, overloaded or headphones?
lab.lat.verdict.ok: Not critical: the offset is below 0.1 s. DT values stay small.
lab.lat.verdict.mid: Noticeable but acceptable. The decoder still finds the signals, DT values are shifted by this amount. Two identical devices see about this DT at each other.
lab.lat.verdict.bad: Too large (over 0.5 s). The windows no longer fit well, the send time needs a compensation.
lab.lat.unsure: The measurement is uncertain (few valid values or large spread), please repeat.
sim.title: Simulator
sim.text: The signal is generated on the device, mixed with time and frequency offset, clock error and noise, and read by the real decoder. No speaker, no microphone. The signal-to-noise ratio refers to 2500 Hz as usual for FT8.
sim.profileNote: Profile: {profile}, set time and tone spacing with the profile chip.
sim.seriesText: Several runs per value with changing noise. The curve shows the success rate, the 50 % threshold is the number to compare profiles by.
sim.estimate: About {n} runs, roughly {time} on this device.
sim.noThreshold: no threshold in range (adjust the range)
sim.gainValue: {db} dB per doubling (expected about 2.5 to 3 dB)
sim.falseWarn: {n} wrong messages decoded, this must not happen.
sim.fewRuns: Only {n} runs per value: the threshold is rough (about ±2 dB). For reliable numbers use at least 6, better 10 runs per value.
cod.intro: From the message to the 79 tones. Everything here is computed with the same modules the app uses for sending, and checked against reference values from WSJT-X (ft8_lib).
cod.c1.title: Message and fields
cod.c1.text: The text is split into fields: callsigns (c28), locator or report (g15) and a few flag bits.
cod.c2.title: 77 bits
cod.c2.text: Each field takes a fixed range of the 77 bits. The label names field, value and position.
cod.c3.title: CRC-14
cod.c3.text: A checksum over the 77 bits (padded with five zeros) appends 14 bits: 91 in total.
cod.c4.title: LDPC (174, 91)
cod.c4.text: 83 parity bits are computed from the 91 bits. The result has 174 bits, more protection than payload.
cod.ldpc.sizes: 91 bits become 174 bits. The {m} parity bits belong to {m} parity equations.
cod.c5.title: Try the error protection
cod.c5.text: Flip bits and watch the decoder set them right again, as long as there are not too many.
cod.flip.hint: Tap bits to flip them (flipped bits are marked with a frame and a strike), or insert random errors. Here the decoder only knows hard bits. The real decoder gets soft values and manages far more. To see the difference to the real decoder switch to “Soft values” at the top.
cod.flip.none: No errors: the codeword satisfies all parity equations.
cod.flip.otherWord: The correction ends at a different valid codeword. Text: {text}. This is rare but possible.
cod.flip.failed: Not correctable: the parity equations stay violated.
cod.flip.history: Violated parity equations after each round
cod.c6.title: Triples and tones
cod.c6.text: The 174 bits are split into 58 triples. Each triple picks one of eight tones through the Gray code.
cod.c7.title: 79 symbols
cod.c7.text: To the 58 data symbols come three Costas blocks of seven symbols each as sync marks: 7 + 29 + 7 + 29 + 7 = 79.
cod.symbols.label: Grid of the 79 symbols, tone 0 to 7 over symbol number
cod.symbols.legend: Filled boxes: data symbols. Frames: Costas blocks (always 3 1 4 0 6 5 2). Swipe to scroll.
cod.c8.title: Signal
cod.c8.text: This is what the signal looks like in a spectrogram when the tones are sent with Gaussian transitions. Time runs downwards.
cod.signal.profile: Profile: signal length {sec} s, tone spacing {spacing} Hz, tone 0 at {f0} Hz
cod.signal.label: Spectrogram of the signal, time downwards, frequency to the right
cod.signal.note: Background: spectrogram of the generated signal (one window per symbol, so smeared in the standard profile). White line: the tones sent, step by step. The numbers below are tones 0 to 7, time runs downwards and follows the selected profile.
cod.err.typ2_nicht_unterstuetzt: Callsigns with /P belong to type 2, which the app cannot do yet.
cod.err.typ4_nicht_unterstuetzt: This callsign needs type 4 (non-standard, with hash), which the app cannot do yet.
cod.err.zu_lang: Free text may have at most 13 characters.
cod.c1.more.1: FT8 never sends text character by character. A standard message such as CQ DL6LG JO60 is split into fields, and each field is stored as a number. The name of a field says what it holds and how many bits it takes: c28 is a callsign (call) with 28 bits, g15 a locator (grid) with 15 bits.
cod.c1.more.2: For type 1 the fields follow in the order c28, r1, c28, r1, R1, g15, i3. The two r1 bits show whether a callsign carries a /R. R1 stands for the “R” in front of a report (R-07), and i3 names the message type. In the example r1 and R1 are zero because there is neither a /R nor a report, and i3 is 1, meaning standard message.
cod.c1.more.3: Free text (up to 13 characters) has its own layout with 71 bits for the text. Messages with /P (type 2) and callsigns that do not fit the standard scheme (type 4, with hash) cannot be packed by the app yet. The input rejects them with a note.
cod.c2.more.1: A standard callsign is brought to six positions, with the digit always at position 3. DL6LG gets a space at the end, K1ABC one at the start. Each position has its own small character set: 37 characters at position 1, 36 at position 2, the ten digits at position 3 and 27 each at positions 4 to 6. The callsign is written as a number in a positional system with mixed bases.
cod.c2.more.2: There are 37 · 36 · 10 · 27 · 27 · 27 = 262,177,560 such callsigns. 28 bits hold 268,435,456 values. The remainder at the lower end is reserved for special cases: DE = 0, QRZ = 1, CQ = 2, then the CQ variants such as CQ DX and the 22-bit hashes. The actual callsigns start at 6,257,896.
cod.c2.more.3: Example DL6LG: the indices of the six positions are 14, 21, 6, 12, 7 and 0. That gives 103,462,785, plus 6,257,896 makes 109,720,681. The card shows this value next to the field.
cod.c2.more.4: The locator sits in g15. A four-character locator has 18 · 18 · 10 · 10 = 32,400 possibilities, 15 bits hold 32,768. The remaining 368 values carry RRR, RR73, 73 and the report, so the report needs no field of its own. JO60 gives ((9 · 18 + 14) · 10 + 6) · 10 + 0 = 17,660. The check for the whole message: 28 + 1 + 28 + 1 + 1 + 15 + 3 = 77 bits.
cod.c3.more.1: The checksum (CRC, cyclic redundancy check) is meant to catch wrong messages. With very weak reception the decoder can find a bit pattern that satisfies all parity equations of the error correction but was never sent. A random pattern hits the right 14-bit checksum with a probability of only 1 : 16,384, about 0.006 %.
cod.c3.more.2: It is computed like a long division, only with bits. The bit string counts as a polynomial and is divided by a fixed generator polynomial (hexadecimal 0x2757, 0x6757 with the leading x¹⁴). The 14-bit remainder is the checksum. Adding means XOR here, there is no carry. Before calculating, WSJT-X appends five zeros to the 77 bits, so the division runs over 82 bits. The card shows exactly this input. One zero more or less would change the result.
cod.c3.more.3: For CQ DL6LG JO60 the result is 13162 (binary 11001101101010). The receiver recalculates the checksum and compares. If it does not match, the message is discarded without asking. It is not completely tight: with very many decoding attempts a false decode occasionally slips through, which is why WSJT-X marks uncertain decodes with a question mark.
cod.c4.more.1: The CRC detects errors, it does not repair any. That is the job of an LDPC code (low-density parity check) named (174, 91): 91 bits go in, 174 bits come out. “Low density” means each bit appears in only a few parity equations, in exactly three for FT8. The parity-check matrix consists almost entirely of zeros, which makes decoding fast.
cod.c4.more.2: The 83 parity bits come from a matrix multiplication over the binary field. A generator matrix with 83 rows and 91 columns is multiplied by the 91 bits, where multiplying means AND and adding means XOR. The 91 input bits stay unchanged at the start of the codeword, the parity bits are appended. Such a code is called systematic. The matrices come from WSJT-X and are in the app in the file constants.js, generated from ft8_lib.
cod.c4.more.3: A matrix with 83 rows and 174 columns does the checking. A bit vector is a valid codeword exactly when all 83 equations hold. All 174 bits count the same, payload bits, CRC bits and parity bits. If a parity bit flips, three equations raise an alarm as well, and the decoder repairs it like a payload bit.
cod.c4.more.4: Of the 174 bits only 77 are payload (44.3 %). 14 belong to the CRC and 83 to the LDPC code, 97 check bits in total (55.7 %). More than half of the transmitted bits serve as control. That is the price for FT8 working well below the noise.
cod.c5.more.1: Here you can experience the error protection yourself. Every bit sits in three parity equations. A single flipped bit therefore raises exactly three alarms, and the decoder resets the bit that fits those alarms. Try a payload bit, a CRC bit and a parity bit, it makes no difference.
cod.c5.more.2: The decoder is called belief propagation. Every bit and every equation exchange assessments, expressed as probabilities. In each round the equations confirm or contradict each other until all 83 hold or 25 rounds are used up. The bars show how many equations are still violated after each round. When the correction works they drop to zero.
cod.c5.more.3: Measured with this card (100 random error patterns per count, message CQ DL6LG JO60): up to 4 flipped bits are always corrected. With 10 it works in about 95 of 100 cases, with 12 in 74, with 15 only in 11, from 20 on not at all. In these measurements no wrong but valid-looking text ever came out.
cod.c5.more.4: The card works with hard bits, every bit counts the same. The real decoder gets more information: for each bit it sees how clearly the tone was received and can separate reliable from unreliable bits. In practice it therefore manages considerably more. If the correction ends at a different valid codeword, the card says so. In real operation the CRC catches such a case.
cod.c6.more.1: The 174 bits are split into 58 triples. Three bits give eight possible values, and FT8 has eight tones (8-FSK). Each triple therefore becomes a tone from 0 to 7.
cod.c6.more.2: The assignment follows a Gray code instead of the binary number: 000 gives tone 0, 001 tone 1, 011 tone 2, 010 tone 3, 110 tone 4, 100 tone 5, 101 tone 6 and 111 tone 7. Neighbouring tones then differ in exactly one bit. If the receiver mistakes tone 3 for tone 4 because of fading or Doppler, only one bit is wrong with the Gray code (010 versus 110). With a binary assignment all three would be wrong (011 versus 100). The LDPC decoder irons out a single bit error.
cod.c6.more.3: The tone determines the frequency: f = f0 + tone · tone spacing. In the standard profile the spacing is 6.25 Hz, so with f0 = 1500 Hz tone 7 lies at 1543.75 Hz. With the tone spacing factor kf the spacing grows.
cod.c7.more.1: There is no common clock between sender and receiver, and the receiver knows neither when a signal starts nor on which frequency it lies. That is why the signal contains a synchronisation pattern, a Costas array of seven tones: 3 1 4 0 6 5 2. It appears three times, at the start, in the middle and at the end, with 29 data symbols in between. That makes 7 + 29 + 7 + 29 + 7 = 79 symbols.
cod.c7.more.2: A Costas array coincides with itself in only one place. Shift it by one step in time or frequency and at most single tones match. The receiver searches for the pattern and derives time and frequency of the signal from it. Because it appears three times, this works even when the start or end is disturbed. 21 of the 79 symbols carry no data, their job is to be found.
cod.c7.more.3: The card shows the sequence as a grid, symbol number horizontally, tone vertically. Frames are Costas symbols (numbers 0 to 6, 36 to 42 and 72 to 78), filled boxes are data symbols (7 to 35 and 43 to 71).
cod.c8.more.1: In the standard profile one symbol lasts 0.16 s, 79 symbols make 12.64 s. The signal starts 0.5 s after the beginning of the 15-second window. With the time factors kt = 2, 4 and 8 everything gets longer accordingly, with the tone spacing factor kf the tone spacing grows. The card shows the signal in the selected profile.
cod.c8.more.2: The tones are not switched hard, because hard jumps would cause phase jumps and wide spurious emissions. FT8 works with continuous phase (CPFSK), and the frequency transitions are smoothed with a Gaussian filter (BT = 2.0). That is why the method is called 8-GFSK. At the start and end the amplitude rises and falls over one eighth of a symbol, 20 ms in the standard profile, to avoid clicks.
cod.c8.more.3: In the standard profile the tone spacing (6.25 Hz) is exactly as large as the symbol rate (6.25 baud). The eight tones are therefore orthogonal over the duration of one symbol: the receiver can separate them cleanly with a Fourier transform although they are only 6.25 Hz apart. The signal occupies 8 · 6.25 Hz = 50 Hz.
cod.c8.more.4: The picture is a spectrogram of the generated signal with a window one symbol long. In the standard profile the traces smear, because such a short window does not separate tones spaced exactly 1/symbol duration apart. The white line therefore shows the tones that were sent. With a larger tone spacing, for example kt = 4 and kf = 2, the traces are clearly separated.
help.unavailable: The help is not available. It is loaded on first use, which needs a connection once.

about.purpose: FT8 for complete QSOs over loudspeaker and microphone, with stretchable time and adjustable tone spacing. Plus a teaching tool that shows the chain from the message to the signal.
about.privacyText: All data stays on this device. There are no accounts and no analytics. The app only asks the server it was loaded from for the time (clock check).
cod.recv.empty: No signal selected yet. In the QSO tab tap the symbol on a line of the band activity or the QSO window, or run a single run of the simulator in the lab and open it from there.
cod.recv.broken: The intermediate values of this signal are incomplete and cannot be shown.
cod.recv.score: Search score of the Costas blocks
cod.recv.heat.label: Power of the eight tones in all 79 symbols, bright means strong, a white dot marks the tone that was sent
cod.recv.heat.legend: Brighter means more power. White dot: the tone that was sent according to the result. Swipe to scroll.
cod.recv.heat.summary: Strongest tone equals sent tone: {all} of 79 symbols (Costas {c} of 21, data {d} of 58).
cod.recv.llr.legend: Number: decision from the sign of the LLR. Blue stands for 0, orange for 1, the more saturated the colour, the more certain the bit. Frame: a bit the correction flipped. Long-press a bit or hover over it to see the LLR value.
cod.recv.llr.summary: Uncertain bits (LLR between −1 and +1): {u} of 174. Bits flipped by the correction: {k}.
cod.recv.bp.none: The first decision from the LLR already satisfies all 83 equations, the correction had nothing to do.
cod.e1.title: Signal found
cod.e1.text: Time, frequency and signal-to-noise ratio with which the decoder found the signal.
cod.e1.more.1: The receiver knows neither the start time nor the frequency of a signal. It slides the Costas pattern over the recording in time and frequency and sums the energy at the places where the three patterns would have a tone. Where the sum stands out of the noise there is a candidate with a preliminary frequency and time offset. The app then refines both values until the energy of the 21 Costas tones is greatest. The accuracy is about 2 to 4 ms and 0.1 to 0.4 Hz.
cod.e1.more.2: DT is the time offset from the expected start (0.5 s after the start of the window), f0 the frequency of tone 0. The signal-to-noise ratio refers to 2500 Hz bandwidth and is estimated from the tone powers. For very strong signals the estimate is too low because the neighbouring tones receive power through the Gaussian transitions. Real recordings with over 40 dB show about 0 to +2 dB there. Keep this in mind for reports.
cod.e1.more.3: The evaluation window says how the tone powers were measured. A Hann window over two symbols lets in less power from neighbouring signals on a busy band, a rectangular window over one symbol is better for pure noise. The app tries both and takes the first result whose checksum matches.
cod.e2.title: Tone powers
cod.e2.text: The power of the eight tones for each symbol. The dot shows the tone that was sent according to the result.
cod.e2.more.1: For each of the 79 symbols the decoder measures the power of the eight possible tones. The recording is multiplied by one complex carrier each of frequency f0 + tone · tone spacing and summed over the duration of one symbol, 0.16 s in the standard profile. Because the tone spacing is exactly 1/symbol duration the tones are orthogonal: a tone that was sent appears only in its own row, the other seven show noise.
cod.e2.more.2: The grid shows the powers, brighter means stronger. The white dot marks the tone that was sent according to the decoded text. With a good signal the brightest spot of each symbol lies under the dot. With a weak signal a noise tone sometimes wins, and the bright spot sits next to it. The error protection has to iron out such symbol errors, and it can as long as not too many bits are affected.
cod.e2.more.3: The Costas symbols sit at fixed places (0 to 6, 36 to 42 and 72 to 78). Below the grid it says in how many symbols the strongest tone was the right one, separately for Costas and data. WSJT-X only lets a candidate pass if at least 7 of the 21 Costas tones match.
cod.e3.title: LLR of the 174 bits
cod.e3.text: The tone powers give a soft value for each of the 174 bits, the LLR.
cod.e3.more.1: The decoder does not commit at once. For each bit it forms a log-likelihood ratio (LLR): the best level in dB of all tones for which the bit is 1, minus the best level of all tones for which it is 0. Positive means more likely 1, negative more likely 0, near zero means unclear. Each symbol delivers three bits, so the levels of the eight tones of one symbol determine three LLRs at once.
cod.e3.more.2: Then all 174 values are brought to a fixed spread (a value taken over from ft8_lib). The grid shows the decision from the sign (blue 0, orange 1), the saturation shows the certainty. A frame marks bits that the correction later flipped against this first decision. These are the bits where the noise struck.
cod.e3.more.3: These soft values are the reason FT8 still works far below the noise. An uncertain bit counts little, a certain one a lot. With hard decisions, as in the card “Try the error protection” of the send direction, much of this information would be lost.
cod.e4.title: Belief propagation
cod.e4.text: The parity equations negotiate until all 83 hold.
cod.e4.more.1: Belief propagation, also called the sum-product algorithm, runs on the LLRs. It works on the factor graph of the code: 174 bits on one side, 83 parity equations on the other, connected wherever the parity-check matrix has a one. An equation tells a bit what the other bits of the equation suggest about its value, the bit sums everything up and passes its assessment back. After each round it decides and checks how many equations are still violated.
cod.e4.more.2: The history shows this number after each round. When it drops to zero all 83 equations hold and the result is a valid codeword. The app stops after 25 rounds. With strong signals a few rounds are enough, with weak ones it takes longer or does not succeed.
cod.e4.more.3: If this fails WSJT-X tries further methods (ordered statistics decoding and decoding with a priori knowledge) and subtracts signals it has found to uncover hidden ones. This app cannot do that yet, signal subtraction and OSD are planned. That is why it finds fewer messages than WSJT-X on a busy band: in a comparison on 60 band recordings it found 67.7 % of the messages on the WSJT-X list.
cod.e5.title: CRC and text
cod.e5.text: Recompute the checksum, unpack the bits, read the message.
cod.e5.more.1: Once a valid codeword is found, the CRC steps in again: the checksum over the 77 payload bits is recomputed and compared with the 14 received CRC bits. If both match, the decode is valid and only then does a message appear. A wrong codeword would get through with a probability of 1 : 16,384.
cod.e5.more.2: Finally the 77 bits are unpacked with the reversed formulas from the send direction: the number in the c28 field becomes the callsign again, g15 the locator. The card shows the fields of the message. With the button at “Signal found” the same message can be viewed in the send direction, where you see the same bits from the other side.
install.title: Install app
install.hint: FT8-Horch can be installed as an app: its own icon, no browser frame, and it works without a network.

install.state.knopf: Install FT8-Horch as an app: its own icon on the home screen, no browser frame, and it starts without a network.
install.state.ios: On iPhone and iPad this is done by hand: tap the share icon of Safari and choose “Add to Home Screen”.
install.state.menue: Your browser does not offer installation by button right now. In Chrome you find it in the menu (three dots) under “Install app” or “Add to home screen”. Some browsers only offer it after a few visits.

time.sourceNote: System time: the device clock as it is. Server time: the app asks the server it was loaded from for the time and compensates the deviation itself, accurate to about 0.1 s and renewed every ten minutes. This helps when the device clock is wrong. Without a network it stays with the system time. The device clock itself is never changed.
time.server.active: Server time active. The device clock deviates by {dev} s (± {unc} s), the app uses the server time.
time.server.none: Server time not available (offline?). The app uses the system time for now.
time.server.unsure: The server time measurement is too imprecise (± {unc} s). The app uses the system time for now.
cod.soft.hint: Here the app simulates a signal with noise and lets two decoders loose on the same disturbance: one that only knows hard bits (0 or 1, each equally certain) and the real way with soft values (LLR). The bits the noise got wrong are framed in the grid.
cod.soft.profile: Profile: time factor kt = {kt} ({sec} s per window). More time makes the same noise less harmful.
cod.soft.legend: Number: hard decision from the sign of the LLR. Blue stands for 0, orange for 1, the more saturated the colour, the more certain the bit. Frame: a bit the noise got wrong. Long-press a bit or hover over it to see the LLR value.
cod.soft.wrongCount: Wrong bits after the first decision: {n} of 174. Violated parity equations: {v} of 83.
cod.soft.hardTitle: Hard bits only (every bit equally certain)
cod.soft.softTitle: With soft values (how the decoder computes)
cod.soft.countResult: At {snr} dB and {n} runs it succeeds {w} times with soft values and {h} times with hard bits. On average {f} bits are wrong.
cod.c5.more.5: Switch the card at the top to “Soft values”. The app then simulates a signal with adjustable noise and hands the same disturbance to the error protection in two ways: once as hard bits only (each bit 0 or 1, equal trust) and once as soft values (LLR, how certain each bit is). The bits the noise got wrong are framed in the grid. Mostly they sit at the pale, uncertain cells. That is exactly what the real decoder uses.
cod.c5.more.6: Measured with this model (standard profile, 200 runs per value): at −18 dB it succeeds in 99 of 100 cases with soft values and in 85 with hard bits, at −19 dB in 85 against 39 and at −20 dB in 30 against 4. On average almost 15 bits are wrong at −19 dB. The same number of randomly flipped bits is managed by the card with hard bits in only about one case in nine, because noise errors almost always sit at the uncertain bits and random errors everywhere. Half of the runs succeed with soft values at about −19.8 dB, which fits the −19.6 dB measured with real signals, with hard bits it is about 1 dB less. At kt = 8 the threshold moves down by about 9 dB, the measurement with real signals gave −27.3 dB there, the simple model is somewhat optimistic here.

wav.title: WAV files
wav.text: Save the recording of the last window as WAV (12 kHz, 16 bit), or load a WAV file and decode it, for example from WSJT-X or an earlier session. The transmit signal can be saved in the Coding tab. Everything stays on the device.
wav.leadNote: Own recordings start 2.5 s · kt before the window; the value is part of the file name and is taken from there. WSJT-X files start with the window (0). Time factor and tone spacing come from the file name, otherwise from the current profile.
wav.needMic: The microphone is off, there is no recording.
wav.notEnough: The last window was not recorded completely (microphone started later, or the window has not ended yet).

auto.notify: Notify me of calls to me
auto.holdNote: “Keep” leaves the transmit frequency alone when the app replies to a CQ (auto-reply or tap). “Keep calling CQ” restarts the CQ call in the same window when a QSO ends (73 sent or received, or given up). Stop ends everything.
vt.title: Connection test (two devices)
vt.text: Two devices lie side by side, both with the microphone on and the same profile. Choose “Device A” on one and “Device B” on the other and start the test on both. The app shows the start time (UTC); it must be the same on both devices, otherwise cancel and start again. A sends a short text in the even windows, B in the odd ones, both measure signal-to-noise ratio and DT. At the end each device sends a summary, so both directions are shown on both devices. Duration with 15 s windows: (2 · rounds + 4) · 15 s. QSO operation is locked during the test.
vt.needCall: Enter callsign and locator, otherwise the station does not run (Settings).
vt.locked: The connection test is running, cancel or finish it first.
vt.plan: Start at {time} UTC, in {sec} s. The other device must show the same time; choose the other role there.
vt.profile: Profile: kt={kt}, kf={kf}, transmit frequency {f0} Hz. Both devices need the same profile.
vt.res.out: Device {x} hears this device (report from the other side)
vt.res.clock: Clock of this device against device {x}
vt.verdict.gut: Good: both directions arrive, DT and clock difference are below 0.3 s.
vt.verdict.nichts_empfangen: This device heard nothing from the other. Check volume, distance and microphone.
vt.verdict.nichts_gehoert: The other device heard nothing from this one. Raise the volume of this device, reduce the distance.
vt.verdict.rate_ein: This device decoded fewer than three of four messages from the other.
vt.verdict.rate_aus: The other device decoded fewer than three of four messages from this one.
vt.verdict.latenz_hoch: The mean DT is larger than 0.3 s: the latencies of the devices are too large (see delay measurement).
vt.verdict.uhr_unterschied: The clocks of the two devices differ by more than 0.3 s (or the latencies are unequal). Use the time source and clock check in Settings.
vt.verdict.keine_zusammenfassung: The summary of the other device did not arrive. The numbers for the other direction are on the other device.
